# Teaching agents taste: how design skills de-slop AI interfaces

> Skills like frontend-design, taste-skill and impeccable package opinions as files agents load on demand. Here is how to combine them.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/taste-and-skills-for-agents/>

An agent skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file that the agent reads when a task matches the skill's description. For design work this matters more than it sounds: opinions about spacing, motion and what never to ship survive between sessions, instead of living in one long prompt you paste every morning. This post explains how skills load, which kinds of design skill are worth having, how to combine them without conflicts, and how to write a small project skill of your own.

## How a skill is loaded

A skill starts with a short YAML header, a `name` and a `description`, followed by instructions in Markdown. Agents that support skills, such as Claude Code, read only the name and description of every installed skill up front. The full body is loaded when the current task matches the description. Extra files in the folder (reference docs, scripts, examples) are read only when the body points to them.

That design has two consequences for you:

- **The description is the trigger.** "Design helper" never fires at the right time. "Use when building or restyling a web page or component; enforces our type scale, spacing and banned patterns" does.

- **Bodies can be long, but should be layered.** Put the rules the agent always needs in `SKILL.md`, and move long references (the full token table, component examples) into separate files it can open on demand.

---
name: house-ui
description: Use when creating or restyling any web page or UI component in this repo. Enforces tokens, spacing, motion limits and banned patterns.
---
# House UI rules
1. Read tokens.css before writing styles. Never use raw hex colours.
2. Spacing comes from the 4px scale: 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64.
3. One accent colour per screen. Body text max 68ch.
4. Motion: 150–250ms, ease-out, transform/opacity only; honour prefers-reduced-motion.
5. Never: gradient text, glassmorphism cards, emoji icons, centred body copy.
For component examples, open examples.md.

## Four jobs, four kinds of skill

Design skills fall into four jobs. Mixing two skills that do the same job is where conflicts come from.

- **Direction** — runs 
before
 code. It commits to an aesthetic and bans the generic tells. Examples: 
frontend-design
 from Anthropic's skills repository, 
taste-skill
.

- **Craft** — runs 
while
 building. It carries judgement about motion, micro-interaction and detail. Example: 
emil-design-eng
.

- **Audit** — runs 
after
 a draft exists. It checks against named rules and reports problems. Examples: 
impeccable
, 
baseline-ui
, 
web-design-guidelines
.

- **Redesign** — runs on an 
existing
 site. It inventories what is there before changing it. Example: 
redesign-skill
.

## A working stack, step by step

**Step 1: install one skill per job.** One direction, one craft, one audit skill per project is enough. Two direction skills will argue about whether the page should be editorial or brutalist, and the agent will average them into neither.

**Step 2: write project rules in AGENTS.md.** Generic taste skills do not know your brand. AGENTS.md is a plain Markdown file at the repo root that coding agents read for project instructions. Put the hard rules there, and say explicitly that they win over any skill:

## Design rules (override any installed skill)
- Brand accent is #2563eb; do not introduce a second accent.
- Headings use Instrument Serif; body uses Geist.
- Light and dark themes are both required for every screen.
- Max one animated "hero moment" per page.

**Step 3: run the direction skill first.** Ask the agent to propose a direction in words before any code: palette, type pairing, layout idea, the one thing that will make the page memorable. Approve or correct it.

**Step 4: build with the craft skill active.** Let it handle hover, focus and transition details, and keep your AGENTS.md limits on motion in force.

**Step 5: audit, then fix in named items.** Run the audit skill on the result and ask for a numbered list of problems with file and line. Fix them in small batches, not all at once.

## Pitfalls

- **Loading everything.** Ten design skills means ten sets of advice competing for the same decisions. More skills is not more taste.

- **Vague descriptions.** If the description does not match how you phrase tasks, the skill never loads and you will think it does not work.

- **Rules only in chat.** A rule you typed once disappears next session. If you repeat it twice, it belongs in AGENTS.md or a skill.

- **Audit before direction.** Auditing a page with no committed direction produces a list of nitpicks on a generic layout.

- **Copying a skill without reading it.** Skills can run scripts. Read the files before you install one, the same way you would read a dependency.

## Questions we get

**Do skills replace a design system?** No. A skill tells the agent how to use your design system and what to avoid. The tokens and components still have to exist; the skill points at them.

**How long should a project skill be?** Short enough that you would read it yourself: 20–40 lines of rules in `SKILL.md`, with longer material in linked files. If the agent ignores a rule, the usual cause is that it was buried in a long list, not that the list was too short.

**How do we know a skill is working?** Give the agent a task that should trigger it and ask it which skills it used. Then check the output against two or three rules from the skill. If the skill never fires, rewrite the description using the exact words you use for tasks.

**Can different agents share the same skills?** Several coding agents now read skill folders or AGENTS.md. Keep the rules in plain Markdown with no tool-specific syntax, and the same files can serve more than one agent. Check each agent's documentation for where it looks.

**What about public skills that change?** Pin the version you reviewed. Treat an update like a dependency upgrade: read the diff before you accept it.

## Our take

Skills turn taste from a prompt into infrastructure. The most valuable one in most repos is not a famous public skill but a 30-line project skill that encodes your tokens and your "never" list. Start there, add one public skill per job, and remove any skill that you notice giving advice you keep overriding.

## Checklist

- Each skill has a description that matches how you phrase tasks

- One direction, one craft, one audit skill per project

- Project rules in AGENTS.md, marked as overriding skills

- Direction agreed in words before code

- Audit output is a numbered list with file and line

- Every installed skill has been read before use

## References
- [Agent Skills repository](https://github.com/anthropics/skills) — Anthropic
- [taste-skill](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill) — Leonxlnx
- [impeccable](https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable) — Paul Bakaus
- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md) — agents.md
- [Web Interface Guidelines](https://vercel.com/design/guidelines) — Vercel
- [Agent Skills overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview) — Anthropic
- [Skills in Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) — Anthropic

# Component composition: why headless + copy-paste won

> Radix behaviour, your styles, code you own. Compound components keep APIs small and make AI edits safer.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/component-composition/>

The old model of a component library was a styled npm package: you installed it, then fought its styles with overrides and `!important`. shadcn/ui flipped that. Behaviour and accessibility come from headless primitives such as Radix, styling comes from Tailwind classes, and the component source is copied into your repository, where you own it. This post explains why that composition model suits AI agents unusually well, how to structure the layers, and the patterns that keep generated code maintainable.

## Three layers, three owners

Think of your UI in three layers, each with a different rate of change and a different owner:

- **Primitives** — headless, accessible behaviour: focus management, keyboard handling, ARIA wiring, portals. Radix Primitives, React Aria and Ark UI live here. You rarely edit them.

- **Your kit** — styled components built on primitives: `Button`, `Dialog`, `Select`, `Card`. This is what shadcn/ui gives you as source. You edit it occasionally, when the design system changes.

- **Blocks and pages** — compositions of kit components: a pricing section, a settings form, a dashboard header. This changes every week.

Brad Frost's atomic design described a similar split years ago (atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, pages). The practical rule for AI work is simple: **let agents work mostly at the block layer, carefully at the kit layer, and almost never at the primitive layer.**

## Why this suits agents

- **Visible context.** Code in your repo can be read. An agent asked to "add a destructive variant to Button" can open `button.tsx`, see the existing variants and follow the pattern. With a closed npm package it can only guess at props.

- **Small surfaces.** Compound components split one complex widget into parts with narrow responsibilities, so edits are local and predictable.

- **Registries.** A registry lets any project install the same component with one command, so an agent building a new app reuses your kit instead of writing a fresh one.

## Pattern 1: compound components

A compound component exposes parts that share state through context, instead of one component with forty props. Compare:

// monolith: every new need becomes another prop
<Dialog title="Delete project" description="This cannot be undone."
  confirmLabel="Delete" cancelLabel="Cancel" danger showClose
  onConfirm={remove} footerAlign="end" />

// compound: parts you can rearrange, omit or extend
<Dialog>
  <DialogTrigger asChild><Button variant="outline">Delete</Button></DialogTrigger>
  <DialogContent>
    <DialogHeader>
      <DialogTitle>Delete project</DialogTitle>
      <DialogDescription>This cannot be undone.</DialogDescription>
    </DialogHeader>
    <DialogFooter>
      <DialogClose asChild><Button variant="ghost">Cancel</Button></DialogClose>
      <Button variant="destructive" onClick={remove}>Delete</Button>
    </DialogFooter>
  </DialogContent>
</Dialog>

The compound version is longer, but every part is obvious, and adding a checkbox ("also delete backups") means inserting one element, not designing a new prop.

## Pattern 2: `asChild` instead of wrapper soup

Radix's `asChild` prop merges a primitive's behaviour into its child element instead of rendering an extra DOM node. `<DialogTrigger asChild><Button/></DialogTrigger>` gives you one `<button>` with the trigger's ARIA attributes and event handlers, not a button nested inside another button. Nested interactive elements are one of the most common accessibility bugs in generated code, so tell your agent to use `asChild` whenever it wraps a kit component in a primitive part.

## Pattern 3: variants as data

shadcn/ui components describe styling options with class-variance-authority. Variants become a small, readable table instead of conditional class strings scattered through JSX:

const buttonVariants = cva(
  "inline-flex items-center justify-center rounded-md text-sm font-medium focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 disabled:opacity-50",
  {
    variants: {
      variant: {
        default: "bg-primary text-primary-foreground hover:bg-primary/90",
        outline: "border border-input bg-background hover:bg-accent",
        destructive: "bg-destructive text-destructive-foreground hover:bg-destructive/90",
      },
      size: { sm: "h-8 px-3", md: "h-9 px-4", lg: "h-10 px-6" },
    },
    defaultVariants: { variant: "default", size: "md" },
  }
);

Agents edit tables like this reliably. Ask for a new variant and you get one new line, using your existing token classes.

## A step-by-step workflow for adding a block

- **Inventory first.** Ask the agent to list which kit components the new block needs and which are missing.

- **Add missing kit pieces deliberately.** Install them from the shadcn registry or your own, then review them once. Do not let a block quietly invent its own button.

- **Compose the block** only from kit components and layout utilities. No raw `<div onClick>`.

- **Check states and keyboard.** Tab through the block. Open and close every popover with the keyboard. Check focus returns to the trigger.

- **Promote repeats.** If the same composition appears in three blocks, promote it into the kit with a name.

## Pitfalls

- **Editing primitives to fix styling.** Styling belongs in the kit layer. Forking a primitive loses upstream accessibility fixes.

- **Prop explosion in the kit.** If `Card` has 15 boolean props, it wants to be a compound component.

- **Duplicated kits.** Agents happily generate a second `Button` in a feature folder. Search for duplicates in review.

- **Mixing primitive libraries.** Radix for dialogs and another library for popovers means two focus-management models. Pick one per project where possible.

- **Losing the source of truth.** Once copied, components drift from upstream. Keep a note of which upstream version you started from.

## Questions we get

**Should we use shadcn/ui or a packaged library like MUI?** If you want agents to edit components and you care about owning the look, source-in-repo kits are easier. If you want upstream updates with no maintenance and accept the library's look, a packaged library is fine. Mixing both in one product is the expensive option.

**How do we stop agents from editing primitives?** Say it in AGENTS.md, keep primitives in a clearly named folder, and add a CODEOWNERS rule or a CI check that flags changes there. Agents follow folder conventions well when they are written down.

**When should a block become a kit component?** When it appears in three places, has a clear name, and its variations can be described as a short variants table. Before that, duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.

**What about non-React stacks?** The same three layers apply. Vue and Svelte have headless primitive libraries too, and the rule "agents compose blocks, carefully edit the kit, leave primitives alone" does not depend on the framework.

## Our take

The composition model is the reason shadcn-style kits became the default target for AI UI tools: the source is local, the parts are small and the variants are data. Keep the three layers explicit in your folder structure, tell your agent which layer it is allowed to touch, and most "AI made a mess of my components" problems disappear.

## Checklist

- Folders reflect primitives / kit / blocks

- Agents compose blocks only from kit components

- Compound components instead of many-prop monoliths

- `asChild` used when a primitive part wraps a kit component

- Variants defined as data (cva or similar)

- Keyboard and focus checked on every new block

# Dark mode done right: tokens, elevation and contrast

> Dark mode is a second palette, not an inverted one. Use semantic tokens, lighter surfaces for elevation, and desaturated accents.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/dark-mode-done-right/>

Inverting colours is the fastest way to ship a bad dark mode: pure black backgrounds, glowing saturated blues, borders that vanish and shadows nobody can see. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and web.dev both treat dark mode as its own design pass, not a filter. This post covers the token structure that makes two themes cheap, the rules for surfaces, colour and contrast, a step-by-step implementation without the white flash, and what to check before you ship.

## Start from semantic tokens

The single decision that makes dark mode manageable is naming colours by **role**, not by value. Components use `--bg`, `--surface`, `--ink`, `--muted`, `--line` and `--accent`. Each theme assigns values to those roles. A component never knows which theme it is in.

:root, [data-theme="light"] {
  color-scheme: light;
  --bg: #f5f6fa;  --surface: #ffffff;  --raised: #ffffff;
  --ink: #0a0c14; --muted: #4a5164;    --line: rgb(10 12 20 / .10);
  --accent: #2563eb;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --bg: #06070b;  --surface: #0d0f15;  --raised: #151924;
  --ink: #f3f5fb; --muted: #a6adbf;    --line: rgb(255 255 255 / .10);
  --accent: #67e8f9;
}
.card { background: var(--surface); color: var(--ink); border: 1px solid var(--line); }

If your codebase has `#fff` and `text-gray-900` scattered through components, the first step of a dark mode project is replacing them with roles. Agents are good at this mechanical refactor when you give them the role table.

## Rules for surfaces and colour

- **Off-black, not black.** Pure `#000` behind white text maximises halation (the glow around bright text) on many screens. A very dark blue-grey such as `#06070b` reads as black and is easier on the eyes.

- **Off-white text.** `#f3f5fb` instead of `#ffffff` for body text; reserve pure white for small emphasis if at all.

- **Elevation by lightness.** In light mode, shadows separate layers. In dark mode, shadows barely show, so raised surfaces get slightly 
lighter
: background, then surface, then raised. Material's dark theme guidance uses the same idea.

- **Desaturate and lighten accents.** A saturated `#2563eb` that works on white vibrates on near-black. Pick a lighter, less saturated accent for dark, and check it as text and as a button fill separately.

- **Borders carry more weight.** With weak shadows, a 1px translucent line is often what separates cards from the background.

- **Images and illustrations.** Logos and diagrams with white backgrounds become glaring rectangles. Provide dark variants or put them on a neutral surface.

## Contrast in both themes

WCAG asks for at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components. Check muted text, placeholder text, disabled states and links in **both** themes. The usual failure is muted grey that passes on white and fails on near-black, or the reverse.

## Step by step: implementing the switch

**Step 1: respect the system, remember the choice.** Default to `prefers-color-scheme`, let the user override it, and store the override.

**Step 2: set the theme before first paint.** A tiny inline script in `<head>` avoids the white flash on load:

<script>
  try {
    const saved = localStorage.getItem("theme");
    const sys = matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches ? "dark" : "light";
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = saved || sys;
  } catch (e) {
    document.documentElement.dataset.theme = "light";
  }
</script>

**Step 3: set `color-scheme`.** It tells the browser to render form controls, scrollbars and the default canvas in the right theme. Without it you get light scrollbars on a dark page.

**Step 4: consider `light-dark()`.** Modern browsers support the CSS `light-dark()` function, which picks a value based on the active `color-scheme`. It is handy for one-off values: `border-color: light-dark(#e5e7eb, #262a35);`.

**Step 5: wire the toggle.** Update `data-theme`, save the choice, and update `aria-pressed` or the label so screen-reader users know the current state.

## A five-minute dark-mode review

Open the page in dark mode on a real phone at low brightness and on a laptop at full brightness. Look for four things: text that glows or blurs at the edges (too much contrast, often pure white on pure black), cards that disappear into the background (missing border or lightness step), accent colours that vibrate, and any white rectangle (an image, embed or code block that was never themed). Then switch themes with the toggle and reload: the page should come back in the theme you chose, without a flash.

## Pitfalls

- **Inverting with a filter.** `filter: invert(1)` flips photos and brand colours too.

- **Forgetting third-party embeds.** Code blocks, maps, charts and iframes often stay light. Theme them or frame them.

- **Shadows as the only separator.** They disappear in dark mode; add borders or lightness steps.

- **Testing only one theme.** Every screenshot review, visual test and design critique should include both.

- **Theme flash.** Setting the theme in a framework effect after hydration flashes the wrong theme on every load.

## Questions we get

**Should dark mode be the default?** Follow the system setting by default. Users who prefer dark have usually already said so at the operating-system level, and the same goes for light. A manual toggle covers everyone else.

**Do we need a separate dark design in Figma?** You need dark values for every role token and a review of key screens in dark. You do not need to redraw every screen if components use role tokens; the theme swap does the work.

**What about charts and data visualisation?** Chart palettes need their own dark variants. Colours that are distinguishable on white can merge on near-black, so check categorical colours side by side in both themes, and never rely on colour alone to distinguish series.

**How do we keep the two themes from drifting?** Run visual regression screenshots in both themes and fail the build on unexpected changes. Treat a component that looks wrong in one theme as a bug, not a polish item.

**Is "dim" or high-contrast a third theme?** If users need it, yes, and the role-token structure makes it a third column of values. Respect `prefers-contrast` before inventing a custom option.

## Our take

NN/g's research shows preference between dark and light is split and situational, so ship both and remember the choice. The cost of the second theme is almost entirely in the token structure: get roles right and dark mode is a second column of values. UI Hub stores light and dark preview screenshots for each component for exactly this reason; a component that only looks good in one theme is half finished.

## Checklist

- Components use role tokens only; no raw colours

- Off-black background, off-white text, lighter raised surfaces

- Dark-specific accent checked as text and as fill

- 4.5:1 text contrast verified in both themes

- Theme set before first paint; `color-scheme` set

- System preference respected and user override remembered

## References

- [prefers-color-scheme: Hello darkness, my old friend](https://web.dev/articles/prefers-color-scheme) — web.dev (Thomas Steiner)
- [Dark Mode vs. Light Mode: Which Is Better?](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/dark-mode/) — Nielsen Norman Group
- [Dark mode](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/dark-mode) — Tailwind CSS
- [color-scheme](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/color-scheme) — MDN
- [light-dark()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Values/color_value/light-dark) — MDN
- [Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html) — W3C WAI
- [Color system overview — Material 3](https://m3.material.io/styles/color/system/overview) — Google
- [prefers-contrast](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@media/prefers-contrast) — MDN

# v0 in practice: from a prompt to shadcn code you can keep

> v0 is strongest when you treat it as a shadcn/Tailwind code generator, not a design oracle. Brief it like an engineer, then pull the code into your repo.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/v0-prompt-to-shadcn/>

v0 by Vercel generates React components built on shadcn/ui and Tailwind CSS. That stack choice is the whole point: the output is ordinary, readable code using primitives many teams already ship, so the result can leave the tool. Treat v0 as a fast pair-programmer for UI, and judge it by whether you would merge its code.

## A brief that works

- **Name the components.** "Use Card, Tabs and a Table with a sticky header" beats "make a nice dashboard". v0 knows the shadcn vocabulary, so use it.

- **Give tokens, not adjectives.** Radius, one accent colour, font, density. "Modern" means nothing to a model; `--radius: 0.5rem` does.

- **List the states.** Empty, loading, error, long text. Generators default to the happy path.

- **Paste real content.** Lorem ipsum hides layout bugs; real names and prices expose them.

## Iterate in small, named steps

Ask for one change per turn ("tighten the table to 40px rows; keep everything else"). Big rewrites tend to regress parts you already liked. When something is right, say so explicitly so it stays.

## Getting the code out

v0 lets you add generated code to a project through the shadcn CLI or download it, and it deploys to Vercel. Whichever path you take, review it like a PR: check that colours come from CSS variables rather than hard-coded hex, that interactive elements are real buttons and links, and that focus styles exist.

## Our take

v0's ceiling is your brief and your design system. Teams that already use shadcn get the most out of it because the output drops straight into their codebase. Pair it with a taste skill or the guidelines in our encyclopedia to avoid the generic "centred hero + three cards" result.

# Lovable and Bolt: when prompt-to-UI becomes prompt-to-app

> Both tools build whole apps, so design quality now competes with data, auth and deploys for attention. How to keep the look from being an afterthought.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/lovable-bolt-prompt-to-app/>

Lovable and Bolt (by StackBlitz) sit one step beyond component generators: you describe an app and they scaffold front end, routing and, through integrations such as Supabase, a backend. Bolt runs the dev environment in the browser on StackBlitz's WebContainers. The design question changes accordingly: the model is juggling schema, auth and deploys, so visual decisions get made by default unless you make them first.

## A notable change this month

On 8 October 2026 Lovable's changelog removed the three "design directions" it used to show before the first build of a visually open-ended prompt. It now derives the look from your description and asks about colour, typography and layout only when the prompt leaves them open. In practice: **your prompt is now the art brief**. If you don't write one, you get the default.

## Front-load the look

- Open with a style paragraph before any feature list: palette, type, radius, density, one reference site.

- Ask for a static UI pass first, with fake data, and approve it before wiring the backend.

- Keep a `design.md` or similar guideline file in the project and tell the tool to follow it on every change.

- After each feature, check the new screens against that file; drift creeps in one screen at a time.

## When to pick which

Use these tools when you need a working prototype with real data paths fast. Use a component generator (v0, Magic Patterns) or hand-built code when the deliverable is a polished interface inside an existing codebase. Many teams do both: prototype the flow in an app builder, rebuild the final UI with their own system.

> Figma Make turns prompts into working prototypes; the Figma agent, generally available since 6 Oct 2026, reads team guideline files. Why the guideline file matters most.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/figma-make-and-figma-agent/>

Figma Make, introduced at Config 2025, generates interactive prototypes and simple apps from a prompt, and can start from an existing Figma frame. It answered the question designers kept asking about v0-style tools: "can I do this where my designs already live?"

## The agent goes GA

On 6 October 2026 Figma made its product-design agent generally available, after a beta that began in May. Two additions stand out in the coverage: library owners can supply guidelines (markdown files) that the agent reads whenever that library is enabled, and teammates can watch the agent's activity live on the canvas.

## Why the guideline file is the real feature

- It moves art direction from a per-session prompt into a file the team maintains and reviews.

- It makes AI output consistent across people, not just across one person's sessions.

- It is the same pattern as SKILL.md, Cursor rules and Lovable project knowledge: **durable, versioned design context**.

## What to put in yours

Token names and when to use each; spacing and type scales; component do/don't pairs; voice and tone for UI copy; a short "never" list (no text gradients, no emoji icons, no centred body text). Keep it short enough that a reviewer actually reads it, and link to examples rather than describing them. Our encyclopedia's spec digests are a reasonable starting template.

# MagicOS: Magic Patterns bets on an infinite canvas of AI threads

> Launched 13 Oct 2026: one coordinator chat spawns parallel design threads on a shared canvas. What it fixes (lost context) and when a single design is still better.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/magic-patterns-magicos/>

Magic Patterns started as a prompt-to-UI tool aimed at product teams (it launched on Hacker News as YC W23, intentionally front-end only). On 13 October 2026 it introduced MagicOS, which reorganises the product around an infinite canvas rather than one chat and one preview.

## How it is structured

- **Canvas:** everything is a file on it: designs, documents, images, GitHub repos, notes.

- **Coordinator:** the chat you talk to. It answers small questions and turns real work into threads.

- **Threads:** each is an agent doing one piece of work; they run in parallel and report back.

- **Sidebar:** threads by status, so you see what is waiting on you.

## What problem it targets

Anyone who has explored five directions in five chat tabs knows the pain: you repeat the brief in each, lose rejected options, and forget why you picked one. MagicOS keeps PRDs, references, variants and rejected directions side by side, and the coordinator reads the canvas so you explain less. It also offers real-time voice and an MCP server so Claude, Cursor or Codex can build from what is on the canvas.

## When not to use it

Magic Patterns' own docs say a single design still fits better for one page or a quick prototype, and that some features (Plan Mode, Controls, forking, merging, inline comments) were single-design only at launch. Our take: use the canvas for exploration-heavy work, keep the single design for focused polish.

# Aceternity UI deep dive: spectacle, used sparingly

> Copy-paste React + Tailwind + Motion effects that made the "fancy" landing look popular. Which pieces carry a page and which turn it into a demo reel.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/aceternity-ui-deep-dive/>

Aceternity UI, created by Manu Arora, is a collection of copy-paste components built with React, Tailwind CSS and Motion (formerly Framer Motion). It is known for showpiece effects: spotlight and beam backgrounds, 3D cards, animated grids, parallax hero scrolls. Free components are open to copy; there is also a paid tier of templates and blocks.

## What works on real pages

- **One ambient background** behind the hero (grid, dots, a soft spotlight). It adds depth without competing with copy.

- **Bento grids and feature sections** with restrained hover motion.

- **Text reveal or typewriter** for a single headline, not for paragraphs.

## What to avoid

Stacking three effects in one viewport, animating body text, and 3D tilt on cards that hold data. These read as a demo reel and cost performance on low-end phones. Always respect `prefers-reduced-motion`, which several effects do not handle by default, so wrap them yourself.

## How we use it in UI Hub

Aceternity is one of the references behind the user's "restrained fancy" house style: borrow one signature effect per page, keep typography and spacing doing the heavy lifting. Search "aceternity" in the hub to see every Aceternity component we index with a live preview.

# Magic UI deep dive: animated components that install like shadcn

> An open-source (MIT) set of motion components distributed through the shadcn registry. Best picks for SaaS pages and how to keep them accessible.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/magic-ui-deep-dive/>

Magic UI is an open-source library of animated components (MIT licence) designed as a companion to shadcn/ui. Components are added with the shadcn CLI from Magic UI's registry, so the source lands in your repo where you can edit it, rather than living in a dependency.

## Picks that earn their place

- **Marquee** for logo walls and testimonials: motion that carries information.

- **Number ticker** for a single headline metric.

- **Animated beam / orbiting circles** to show integrations, one per page.

- **Shimmer or border-beam buttons** for exactly one primary CTA.

## Accessibility and performance

Continuous motion (marquees, orbits) should pause on hover and stop under `prefers-reduced-motion`; WCAG 2.2.2 asks for a way to pause anything that moves for more than five seconds. Prefer transform and opacity animations, which browsers can composite cheaply.

## Our take

Magic UI is the easiest way to add motion to a shadcn project because it shares the install model and the token variables. The risk is the same as any effects library: use one or two components per page, and let the rest of the UI stay calm.

# Cult UI deep dive: tactile components with personality

> shadcn-compatible components that feel physical: dynamic islands, textured buttons, expandable cards. How to borrow personality without breaking consistency.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/cult-ui-deep-dive/>

Cult UI is an open-source collection of shadcn-compatible components with a distinctly tactile feel: a dynamic-island style container, textured buttons, expandable cards and playful toolbars. Where Aceternity leans on spectacle (beams, spotlights, backgrounds), Cult UI leans on **interaction feel**: springs, squish and layout animation. This deep dive covers what is in the collection, how to adopt a component without breaking your design system, a step-by-step integration, and where personality components go wrong.

## What kind of library it is

Like shadcn/ui itself, Cult UI is not a package you import wholesale. You take individual components into your repository, either by copying the source from the documentation or with the shadcn CLI using the registry address shown on each component's page, and then you own the code. The components are written in React with Tailwind CSS, and most of the interesting ones use Motion for layout and spring animation.

That model matters for AI work. Because the source lands in your repo, an agent can read how the dynamic island morphs between sizes and adapt it, instead of guessing at the props of a black box.

## Where it shines

- **Small product surfaces** that benefit from springy layout transitions: toolbars, popovers, status pills, a recording indicator that expands into controls.

- **Portfolio and indie-product pages** where personality is the point and one memorable interaction is worth more than a polished but generic hero.

- **Learning material.** Reading the source of an expanding card is one of the fastest ways to understand Motion's `layout` and shared-element transitions.

## Where it does not

- **Dense, data-heavy tools.** A squishy button in a table with 200 rows is noise.

- **Frequent actions.** If a control is used dozens of times a day, the spring that delights on day one slows the user down by day ten.

- **Teams without a token system.** Personality components bring their own colours, radii and shadows. Without tokens to map them onto, the product quickly looks like a collage.

## Step by step: adopting one component

**Step 1: choose one signature interaction.** Decide which single interaction should carry the product's personality, for example "the status pill expands into a mini player". One is enough.

**Step 2: install it into your kit folder.** Bring the component in via its docs page or the shadcn CLI and put it next to your other kit components, not inside a feature folder, so there is exactly one copy.

**Step 3: map its styling to your tokens.** Replace hard-coded colours, radii and shadows with your variables:

// before (as copied)
<div className="rounded-[28px] bg-black text-white shadow-2xl">

// after (mapped to your system)
<div className="rounded-[var(--radius-xl)] bg-[var(--raised)] text-[var(--ink)] border border-[var(--line)]">

**Step 4: unify the motion.** Personality components often each ship their own spring. Pick one or two spring presets and use them everywhere, so all motion feels like one family:

// motion.ts
export const spring = {
  snappy: { type: "spring", stiffness: 500, damping: 40 },
  soft:   { type: "spring", stiffness: 260, damping: 30 },
} as const;

**Step 5: add accessibility the demo skipped.** Custom toggles and islands need a real `<button>` or the correct role, visible focus, keyboard support, and `aria-expanded` when they open. Announce state changes with a live region if content changes without focus moving.

**Step 6: respect reduced motion.** Motion's `useReducedMotion` hook lets you swap springs for instant or fade transitions:

import { motion, useReducedMotion } from "motion/react";

export function Island({ open }: { open: boolean }) {
  const reduce = useReducedMotion();
  return (
    <motion.div
      layout
      transition={reduce ? { duration: 0 } : { type: "spring", stiffness: 500, damping: 40 }}
      aria-expanded={open}
    />
  );
}

## Measuring whether it helps

A signature interaction should earn its place. After shipping, watch two things for a couple of weeks: whether people use the control more or less than the plain version it replaced, and whether support questions or bug reports mention it. Record the screen on a mid-range phone as well; spring animations that feel crisp on a laptop can drop frames on cheaper hardware. If the interaction slows people down or confuses them, simplify it rather than adding a second one to compensate. Personality that costs usability is a bad trade.

## Pitfalls

- **Mixing every clever component on one page.** Each one is charming; together they compete for attention.

- **Keeping demo colours.** A component that looks great on the docs' black background can look out of place on your off-white surface.

- **Different springs everywhere.** Ten different stiffness values make the interface feel inconsistent even if users cannot say why.

- **Forgetting mobile.** Hover-driven reveals do nothing on touch screens; give them a tap or always-visible state.

- **Not checking the licence and attribution.** Open-source does not mean no conditions; read the repository's licence before shipping.

## How it compares

Three shadcn-compatible collections cover different ends of the "fancy" range, and knowing which end you need saves a lot of trial and error:

- **Aceternity UI** — spectacle: animated backgrounds, beams, spotlights, 3D cards. Best for a marketing hero.

- **Magic UI** — polished marketing pieces: marquees, number tickers, animated borders, bento grids. Best for landing-page sections.

- **Cult UI** — tactile product details: islands, expandable cards, springy toolbars. Best inside the product itself.

A common and effective combination is one Aceternity- or Magic UI-style moment on the marketing site and one Cult UI interaction inside the app, both mapped onto the same tokens. What does not work is all three on the same page.

## Questions we get

**Will it work with our existing shadcn setup?** Generally yes, since the components follow shadcn conventions and use Tailwind and Motion. Check that your Tailwind version and Motion version match what the component expects before you start mapping styles.

**Can an agent adapt a component to our product?** Yes, and it is a good use of an agent, because the source is local. Give it the component, your tokens and the spring presets, and ask for a diff rather than a rewrite.

**How do we keep it from looking like the demo?** Change the content, colours and size to fit your product, and use the interaction for a real job: showing status, revealing controls, confirming an action.

## Our take

Cult UI is our reference for the "tactile" end of the house-style range: micro-interaction over loud backgrounds. It works best when you pick one signature interaction per product, map it onto your tokens and motion presets, and let it recur. Used that way it gives a product character; used as a grab bag it makes the product feel like a demo.

## Checklist

- One signature interaction chosen; others stay quiet

- Component lives once, in the kit folder

- Colours, radii and shadows mapped to tokens

- Shared spring presets used across components

- Real buttons/roles, focus, keyboard and aria-expanded added

- Reduced-motion fallback in place; licence checked

## References

- [nolly-studio/cult-ui](https://github.com/nolly-studio/cult-ui) — GitHub

# shadcn blocks and registries: page sections as source code

> Blocks (dashboards, sidebars, login pages) install with one CLI command, and any team can publish its own registry. Why this is the best substrate for AI agents.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/shadcn-blocks-deep-dive/>

shadcn/ui is not a package you install; it is a set of components whose source you copy into your project. Blocks extend the idea to whole sections: dashboards, sidebars, login and signup pages, charts. Each is added with the CLI, for example `npx shadcn@latest add dashboard-01`, and lands as editable files.

## Registries: everyone can publish

The shadcn registry format lets any team publish components, blocks, hooks and theme files as JSON that the CLI understands. Magic UI, Cult UI and many others distribute this way, and you can run a private registry for your own design system.

```
npx shadcn@latest add https://your-registry.example/r/pricing-01.json
```

## Why agents love this model

- The code is local, so an agent can read and edit it like any file.

- Names are stable and documented, so prompts can reference them ("add sidebar-07").

- Theme lives in CSS variables, so one token change restyles everything the agent generated.

## Our take

If you want AI-generated UI to stay consistent, give the agent a registry, not a style adjective. Start from official blocks, restyle via tokens, and publish your modified versions to a private registry so every future session builds from your system.

# Typography for AI-generated UI: the fastest way to look less generic

> Generators default to one sans at three sizes. A type scale, a second typeface, tighter tracking on display sizes and real line lengths fix most of it.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/typography-for-ai-generated-ui/>

Ask any generator for a landing page and you will usually get one sans-serif at body, heading and caption sizes. Typography is the cheapest lever to move a page away from that default, and it is easy to specify precisely in a prompt.

## Five rules to put in the brief

- **Use a modular scale.** Pick a ratio (1.2 for dense apps, 1.25–1.333 for marketing) and name the steps as tokens.

- **Pair two typefaces with a job each.** A display face for headlines (a serif such as Instrument Serif, or a tight grotesk) and a workhorse sans for UI.

- **Tighten large text.** Negative letter-spacing (around −0.02em) on display sizes; leave body text at default.

- **Constrain line length.** Roughly 45–75 characters for Latin body text; use `max-width: 65ch`.

- **Fluid sizes.** `clamp()` for headlines so mobile does not inherit desktop sizes.

## CJK needs its own settings

For Chinese and Japanese, use a slightly larger line-height (about 1.7), avoid negative tracking, and use `word-break: keep-all` or `text-wrap: balance` on headings so short phrases are not orphaned, the fix we applied to our own Japanese headings.

## Our take

If you only change one thing in AI output, change the type scale and the display face. It is a two-line token edit with a visible payoff.

entries.summary: OKLCH keeps perceived lightness consistent across hues, so you can generate scales and dark themes by math instead of eyeballing. Tailwind v4 uses it by default.
entries.md:
# OKLCH colour systems: palettes that survive dark mode

> OKLCH keeps perceived lightness consistent across hues, so you can generate scales and dark themes by math instead of eyeballing. Tailwind v4 uses it by default.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/oklch-color-and-dark-mode/>

OKLCH is a CSS colour space (CSS Color Level 4) defined by lightness, chroma and hue. Its lightness channel tracks perceived brightness far better than HSL's, so a yellow and a blue at the same L actually look similarly light. Tailwind CSS v4 switched its default palette to OKLCH, and all modern browsers support `oklch()`.

## Building a scale

```
--brand-50:  oklch(97% 0.02 250);
--brand-500: oklch(62% 0.17 250);
--brand-900: oklch(30% 0.09 250);
```

Keep hue fixed, step lightness evenly, and reduce chroma at the extremes, where sRGB screens cannot display high chroma anyway.

## Dark mode by lightness, not inversion

- Surfaces: very low L (around 14–20%) with a hint of the brand hue instead of pure black.

- Text: high L but not 100%, to reduce glare.

- Accent: raise L and lower chroma slightly so it does not vibrate on dark backgrounds.

- Re-check contrast: equal OKLCH lightness differences do not guarantee WCAG ratios, so test with a contrast checker.

## Our take

Give agents colour tokens in OKLCH with light and dark values side by side. It makes "make it darker" or "add a success colour" a predictable edit instead of a guess.

# Landing page teardown: what Linear and Vercel get right

> Two widely copied developer-tool homepages, read as a list of decisions: one message, product as hero image, dark restraint, and proof placed right after the promise.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/landing-page-teardown-linear-vercel/>

Linear's and Vercel's homepages are among the most imitated in software. Copying their gradients misses the point; what is worth copying is a set of decisions you can see by reading the pages carefully. Screenshots below were captured on 14 October 2026; both sites change often.

## Decisions worth stealing

- **One sentence of positioning** in the hero, large, with a short supporting line. No feature list above the fold.

- **The product is the hero image.** Real UI (or a faithful render of it) instead of an illustration, so the visitor sees what they would use.

- **Restraint in colour.** Mostly neutral surfaces; accent colour reserved for action and emphasis.

- **Proof straight after the promise:** customer logos or concrete product capabilities right below the hero.

- **Sections with one idea each,** each with a short heading and a visual that demonstrates it.

## What not to copy

- Their brand recognition: a minimal hero works when people already know the name; a new product may need a more explicit line.

- Heavy custom motion and 3D renders that took dedicated teams; a static, sharp product shot beats a mediocre animation.

## Checklist for your page

Can a stranger say what you sell after five seconds? Is the first image your actual product? Is there exactly one primary CTA? Does every section prove one claim? If yes, the gradient is optional.

- [Linear homepage](https://linear.app/) — Linear
- [Vercel homepage](https://vercel.com/) — Vercel

# Dashboard patterns that hold up: from KPI strip to drill-down table

> AI tools love to generate twelve charts. Good dashboards answer three questions in order: is it OK, what changed, why. A layout and a component list for each.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/dashboard-design-patterns/>

Ask a generator for an "analytics dashboard" and you will likely get a sidebar, four stat cards and a grid of charts of equal weight. It looks complete and answers nothing. A better structure follows the questions a user actually asks, in order.

## Three layers

- **Is everything OK?** A KPI strip of 3–5 numbers, each with the comparison period and a direction, not a sparkline zoo.

- **What changed?** One primary time-series chart with a range selector, annotated where something happened.

- **Why?** A sortable, filterable table that drills into detail. Tables are where people actually work.

## Details generators skip

- Tabular figures (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`) so numbers align.

- Right-aligned numeric columns, left-aligned text.

- Empty, loading (skeleton) and error states for every widget.

- Units and time zone in labels; a "last updated" timestamp.

- Colour used for status only, with a non-colour cue (icon or text) for colour-blind users.

## Components to start from

shadcn's dashboard blocks and its charts (built on Recharts) give you the scaffolding; Tremor offers dashboard-focused React components. Specify the three layers in your prompt and you get a page people can use, not just screenshot.

# Design tokens for agents: the file that makes AI output on-brand

> A machine-readable token file (the W3C DTCG format) plus a short usage note beats any adjective in a prompt. Structure, naming, and how to hand it to an agent.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/design-tokens-for-agents/>

Agents follow concrete values far more reliably than descriptions. A design token file turns "clean, premium, a bit playful" into numbers the agent can apply everywhere. The W3C Design Tokens Community Group (DTCG) publishes a vendor-neutral JSON format for this, supported by tools such as Style Dictionary and Tokens Studio.

## A minimal structure

```
{
  "color": { "accent": { "$type": "color", "$value": "oklch(62% 0.17 250)" } },
  "radius": { "md": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "10px" } },
  "space": { "4": { "$type": "dimension", "$value": "16px" } }
}
```

## Three tiers of naming

- **Primitive:** raw values (`blue-500`, `space-4`).

- **Semantic:** intent (`surface`, `text-muted`, `accent`, `danger`). Agents should mostly use these.

- **Component:** optional overrides (`button-radius`).

## Handing it to an agent

- Export tokens to CSS variables and commit them; tell the agent "never hard-code colours or spacing, use these variables".

- Add a one-page usage note: which token for which job, plus three do/don't pairs.

- Reference both from your AGENTS.md, Cursor rules or skill so every session loads them.

- Verify: grep generated code for raw hex values as a cheap lint.

Our encyclopedia's colour, spacing and type spec digests are written to be pasted into exactly this kind of usage note.

## References
- [Design Tokens Community Group](https://www.w3.org/community/design-tokens/) — W3C
- [Design Tokens Format Module](https://www.designtokens.org/) — DTCG
- [Style Dictionary](https://styledictionary.com/) — Style Dictionary

# Design skills for Claude and Cursor: SKILL.md, rules and AGENTS.md

> Three file formats, one idea: durable instructions an agent loads when relevant. How to write a design skill that changes output, with a template.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/claude-cursor-design-skills/>

Anthropic's Agent Skills are folders with a `SKILL.md` file: YAML front matter (a name and a description) followed by instructions, optionally with scripts and assets. The agent sees the descriptions and loads a skill's full body only when it is relevant. Cursor offers project rules in `.cursor/rules`, and many coding agents read an `AGENTS.md` at the repo root. Different files, same idea: durable, scoped instructions.

## What makes a design skill work

- **A precise description**, because it decides when the skill loads ("Use when building or restyling web UI").

- **Bans before wishes.** Models respond well to a short list of things never to do (text gradients, emoji icons, centred paragraphs, more than one accent).

- **Concrete values:** tokens, scales, a reference to the token file.

- **A verification step:** "render in a browser at 390px and 1440px, light and dark, before saying done".

## A template

```
---
name: house-ui
description: Use when creating or restyling any web page or component.
---
1. Load tokens from styles/tokens.css. Never hard-code colour/spacing.
2. Type: Instrument Serif display, Geist UI, scale 1.25.
3. Never: text gradients, emoji icons, glassmorphism stacks.
4. One signature effect per page (see /kb/ house style).
5. Verify in a browser: 390/1440px, light/dark, keyboard focus.
```

## Where to find good ones

Anthropic's public skills repository includes a frontend-design skill; community skills such as taste-skill and impeccable focus on aesthetics. Our encyclopedia indexes the ones we use, with full text where the licence allows.

# Tutorial: have an agent build a landing page using UI Hub as context

> Six steps from an empty folder to a verified page: load AGENTS.md, search the encyclopedia, pick components, load skills, build, verify in a browser.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/tutorial-agent-builds-landing-with-ui-hub/>

UI Hub is built to be read by agents: a JSON API, a design encyclopedia with raw Markdown per entry, and an AGENTS.md. This walkthrough shows the loop we use ourselves. Paste the prompts into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any agent that can fetch URLs.

## Six steps

- **Load the guide.** "Read https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/AGENTS.md and follow it."

- **Search the encyclopedia** for the house style and the specs you need: `/kb/?q=house style`, `/kb/?q=typography`.

- **Pick components** from `/api/resources.json`, filtered by type and licence; prefer open-source libraries you can copy.

- **Load skills** in order: a taste or frontend-design skill first, then accessibility and quality checks.

- **Build** with tokens in CSS variables, one signature effect, real copy.

- **Verify in a browser** at 390px and 1440px, light and dark, and fix what you see before reporting done.

## A prompt you can copy

```
Use UI Hub as design context: read /AGENTS.md, search /kb/ for
"house style", "typography", "colour". Build a landing page for
[product] with shadcn + one Aceternity background. Tokens in CSS
variables, 10-language-ready copy, then screenshot 390/1440 light/dark.
```

## Why this works

Each step replaces a vague instruction with a document the agent can read. The 
Agents guide
 has a one-click copy of this prompt in 10 languages, plus a downloadable skill bundle.

# Claude Design everywhere: out of beta, into every chat

> Anthropic took Docs, Slides and Design out of beta on every plan, launched Dashboards and Motion in beta, and will close the standalone Design site on 14 Dec 2026. For UI builders the practical move is to migrate the design system now.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/claude-design-everywhere/>

On 8 October 2026 Anthropic published a product update that matters more for design-and-code workflows than the headline tools might suggest. Claude Dashboards and Claude Motion entered beta; Claude Docs, Slides and Design left beta and are available on every Claude plan, including Free. The same post says the standalone Claude Design site at claude.ai/design stays open only until 14 December 2026, after which design work lives inside ordinary Claude conversations, Claude Code and the Artifacts tab.

## What actually shipped

- **Design in every chat.** Anthropic’s product page and help centre describe Claude Design as an artifact template: describe a visual, get a canvas beside the conversation, then refine with chat, inline comments and on-canvas edits. It works in Claude Code via `/design` and `/design-sync`, and on mobile for viewing and editing (sharing settings stay on web/desktop).

- **Design systems travel with you.** Systems can be imported from GitHub, design files or a local codebase. Teams that used the standalone site can click “Migrate team design systems” on the Artifacts page; Anthropic notes migrated systems may need a “Let Claude clean it up” pass.

- **Dashboards (beta, paid).** Connect Redshift, BigQuery, ClickHouse, Databricks, Snowflake or Salesforce-style connectors, ask in plain language, and get a live dashboard. Each number exposes the query behind it and a refresh time; deeper analysis can be sent to tools such as Amplitude, Grafana, Hex, Mixpanel, Omni, Perplexity, PostHog or Sigma.

- **Motion (beta, Team/Enterprise).** Claude writes code that animates your own text, charts, shapes and images into a short explainer you can edit and export as MP4. Anthropic states it does not use a video-generation model and does not invent footage or people.

- **Enterprise defaults.** Docs, Slides and Design turn on by default on 15 October 2026 (except HIPAA-enabled orgs). Dashboards and Motion stay off until an admin enables them under Organization settings → Artifacts.

## Why it matters for UI builders

The useful shift is not “another AI design toy”. It is that the brief, the design system and the coding agent share one conversation surface. A prototype can start next to a requirements thread, inherit components via `/design-sync`, and hand off to Claude Code without screenshot archaeology. Connectors listed on the product page (Adobe, Canva, Gamma, Lovable, Miro, Replit, Vercel, Wix and others) push the same artifact into the tools you already ship from.

Anthropic’s own announcement claims more than 45 million docs, decks and designs since those templates arrived in every conversation. Treat that as a usage signal, not a quality guarantee: the ceiling is still your tokens, your refuse-list and whether an admin locked a single approved system.

## Our take

Migrate the design system before December, not the day the standalone URL dies. Enterprise teams should treat 15 October as the day Design becomes ambient for everyone who can open Claude—so lock publishing rights and a default system first, or you will get fast, on-brand-looking noise. Prefer Motion when the story is your own data and copy; reach for a dedicated video model when you need filmed scenes. Prefer Dashboards for exploratory questions where seeing the SQL builds trust; keep your BI stack for governed reporting.

## Practical checklist

- Open Artifacts → migrate team design systems; run the clean-up pass on each.

- In Claude Code, run `/design-sync` against the repo that owns tokens and components.

- Write a short house guideline (tokens, type scale, never-list) the same way you would for Figma’s agent or a SKILL.md—Claude Design still needs a file it can obey.

- Enterprise admins: decide before 15 October whether Docs/Slides/Design should stay default-on; enable Dashboards/Motion only after data connectors are reviewed.

- Export path: HTML / PDF / PPTX for stakeholders; hand off to Claude Code or a connector (v0, Vercel, Lovable, Replit…) when the next step is production UI.

- Verify like any generated UI: real content, focus rings, light/dark, 390px and 1440px—not only the canvas preview.

# Figma code layers and Specs: the canvas becomes the shared context again

> At Config India (15 Oct 2026) Figma moved code layers into open beta, launched Specs as a Markdown home on the canvas, and let libraries carry guidelines and code sources. The lesson for UI builders: agents are short of constraint files, not generators.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/figma-code-layers-and-specs/>

On 15 October 2026, at Config India in Bengaluru, Figma shipped a set of updates that are easy to read as “more AI features” and more useful to read as a single idea: put the code, the written intent and the design-system rules on the same canvas, so people and agents work from one context instead of five tabs. Dylan Field’s recap post frames the problem bluntly. AI made code cheap, so teams “build to think”, but that vibe-coding loop is usually single-player; one customer is quoted describing it as “fast, fast, fast… then slow”.

## What launched

- **Code layers, open beta on all plans.** A code layer is a running, interactive prototype that sits on the canvas. You can start one from scratch (Code tool or 
B
), convert selected frames with 
Build selection
, clone a connected GitHub repo, upload a local folder, push a prototype in from your coding tool through the Figma MCP server, or capture a live page with the Chrome extension. Teammates can duplicate a layer to try another direction, comment and annotate it, edit the code, ask the agent to merge the best parts of two versions, pull screens back out with 
Extract designs
, and push to a branch and open a pull request.

- **Specs, open beta on paid plans.** A multiplayer Markdown container that lives as its own file or next to designs in Figma Design and FigJam (press 
D
, or drop any `.md` file on the canvas). A spec can embed frames, FigJam boards and other canvas nodes, the Figma agent can read and reply to comments, and connectors such as GitHub and Hex can pull outside context in. Paste a spec link into a coding agent’s prompt and, according to Figma, the Markdown, frame references, diagrams, code layers and Code Connect snippets travel with it.

- **Design systems that carry rules and code.** Guidelines attached to published libraries (open beta, Professional and above) are handed to the agent automatically whenever someone builds with that library. Code sources (closed beta) attach a GitHub repo or npm package to a library so code layers pull from real components. A centralised design-system space with a system map and a “system check” for gaps such as missing descriptions or interactive states is preview only.

- **Figma MCP.** Figma says the server is now faster and uses fewer tokens; it can create code layers, read and write Specs, generate images and run Weave workflows, and adds tools such as `html_to_figma` and `generate_image`, plus 20 new partner integrations (OpenCode, Dia, Junie, Meta Muse and others).

- **Payload in Figma Make.** Make now scaffolds a Payload backend (CMS, database, auth, APIs, admin panel) as its native backend; Supabase stays available as a third-party connection.

## Why it matters: three shifts

**Prototypes go back to multiplayer.** The real cost of coding-agent prototypes has not been generation; it has been review. A link to a running demo shows the result but hides the alternatives and the reasoning. Putting several running versions side by side on a canvas, with comments pinned to them, restores the critique loop design teams already know. The branch-and-PR exit matters too: the prototype has a route into the repo rather than being rebuilt.

**Markdown finally gets an address.** Most teams working with agents already keep PRDs, `AGENTS.md` files and prompt notes in Markdown, scattered across laptops and repos with no link to the screens they describe. Specs is Figma’s bet that the brief should sit beside the frames, be editable by both humans and agents, and be passable to a coding agent by URL. Whether or not you adopt Specs, the pattern is right: one canonical brief, versioned with the work.

**Design systems become agent-readable.** Guidelines and code sources are the most consequential part of the launch and the least flashy. A library that ships its own do/don’t rules and points at the real npm package turns “please match our design system” from a hope into an input the agent receives every time.

## Our take

The scarce input in AI-assisted UI is still the constraint file. Every tool this month, from Claude Design’s design systems to the Figma agent’s guideline files, has converged on the same lesson: generation is abundant, and quality comes from short, explicit rules about tokens, states and what never to do. Figma is now giving those rules a native place to live and an automatic route to the agent. Teams that already wrote a tight guideline file will see the benefit immediately; teams that skipped it will get faster, on-brand-looking noise.

Two caveats. First, these are betas with staggered rollouts, so features may appear for one teammate before another. Second, cost: code layers use AI credits, free for creating and editing on paid plans only until 4 November 2026, and guidelines can make a prompt more expensive because they add context. Figma’s customer numbers (for example, Merkle reporting 30% faster iteration) are vendor-published snapshots, not independent benchmarks.

## How to try it this week

- **Pick one flow, not a product.** Convert a single real flow (sign-up, checkout, settings) into a code layer from existing frames or a lightweight prototype repo. Duplicate it once to compare two directions.

- **Write a short Spec next to it.** Tokens to use, states that must exist, content rules and a never-list. Keep it to one screen of text so it is actually read.

- **Add guidelines to the library.** Move your do/don’t pairs onto the published library so every agent prompt against it inherits them. If you are in the code-sources beta, attach the npm package your product really ships.

- **Wire MCP from your coding agent.** Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or similar to the Figma MCP server, paste the spec link into the prompt, and let the agent create or update the code layer.

- **Review on canvas like a pull request.** Check empty, loading and error states, long text, keyboard focus and contrast, at 390px and 1440px, before anyone says “ship it”. Then push to a branch.

```
# Spec: Checkout v2
## Tokens
surface / text-muted / accent only; radius 10; Geist 14/20
## States (must exist)
empty cart · loading · card declined · success · long names
## Content
real prices, real error copy; sentence case
## Never
text gradients · emoji icons · placeholder-only labels · raw hex
## Done when
390 + 1440 · light + dark · focus visible · AA contrast
```

## Where UI Hub fits

If you are writing that guideline file or Spec from scratch, start from the design skills and agent guides already collected on UI Hub: filter the resource list by 
skills
 for SKILL.md-style rule files, and see the 
Agents guide
 for the search, pick and verify loop that pairs well with an MCP-connected coding agent. The point is the same whichever canvas you use: give the agent the rules before you ask it for pixels.

# shadcn Trace and AI Elements: one shape for every step an agent takes

> On 14 Oct 2026 shadcn/ui shipped Trace, Code Block and 21 copy-in AI Elements patterns that replace AI SDK Elements. The design lesson: reasoning, tool calls, sources and subagents are all one line with an icon, a title and a status, so agent UIs stop looking like debug logs.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/shadcn-trace-and-ai-elements/>

On 14 October 2026 shadcn published **Trace**, a component for agent activity, together with **Code Block** and **AI Elements**, a set of patterns for agentic interfaces built entirely from shadcn/ui components. The announcement post passed 4,500 likes on X within two days, and shadcn-svelte followed with its own AI Elements a day later. The interesting part is not that there are new components. It is the design claim underneath them: reasoning, tool calls, sources, plans and subagent runs all have the same shape, so they should look and behave the same.

## What shipped

- **Trace.** A list of lines for the steps an agent takes. The shadcn team says it was distilled from studying hundreds of components in agentic interfaces. Each line has an icon, a title, an optional description and a status (`running`, `error` or `pending`, with a shimmer while a step runs). A line can expand, link to a page, or open a dialog, sheet, drawer or popover, and lines can nest, so a summary opens into steps and a step into its output. It reads the reasoning, tool and source parts that the AI SDK streams.

- **Code Block.** Displays code, terminal output, logs and diffs, with a header for a title and actions, line numbers, wrapping, highlighted and diff lines, and a small size (`size="sm"`) meant for tool output inside a Trace.

- **AI Elements, 21 patterns.** Chat, Prompt Input, Reasoning, Tool, Plan, Subagent, Confirmation, Context, Sources, File Tree, Terminal, Test Results and more. There is no package: each pattern is a composition you copy into your repo, and every docs page also exists as Markdown so a coding agent can read it directly.

- **Every base and style.** Trace and Code Block are available for Base UI, React Aria and Radix across all eight shadcn/ui styles, and they join the chat components released in June: Message Scroller, Message, Bubble, Marker, Attachment and Questionnaire.

- **AI SDK Elements is being deprecated.** Code you already copied from elements.ai-sdk.dev keeps working. Each pattern page has a migration prompt that rebuilds the wrapper in `components/ai-elements` on the new components while keeping every export and its props. A few low-usage elements (artifact, audio player, the React Flow canvas pieces, JSX preview, voice and mic selectors) were not rebuilt; the docs list which existing components to compose them from.

## Why it matters: agent UIs get a grammar

Until now most agent interfaces have been assembled one part type at a time: a reasoning accordion here, a tool-call card there, a sources popover somewhere else, each with its own spacing, icon logic and loading state. The result is the familiar “debug log” look, where every turn is a pile of unrelated widgets. Trace replaces that with one row grammar. What changes between a thought, a shell command and a subagent is only the icon, the title and what happens when you open the line.

That grammar also forces good copy. The accessibility notes are unusually specific: the icon is hidden from assistive tech, so the title is the accessible name and should be a sentence that says what happened (“Edited trace.tsx”, not “trace.tsx”). Because status is shown with colour and motion, it also belongs in the words: “Running pnpm build” while it runs, “Failed to run pnpm build” when it errors. The shimmer stops for readers who prefer reduced motion, and inside a Message Scroller each new line is announced once.

The Confirmation pattern adds one more useful rule. A pending approval is a prompt, not activity, so it sits outside the Trace as an item with Deny and Approve buttons, and only becomes a Tool line once the person answers. Asking and doing are visually different things.

## Our take

This is the same move the whole field made this month, from Figma Specs to Claude Design: the useful unit is not a generator but a shared, explicit shape that people and agents can both follow. For agent UIs, Trace is that shape. Teams building copilots, coding agents or research tools should adopt the grammar even if they never install the component, because users judge trust from whether they can see what the agent did, in order, with honest status.

Three caveats. The patterns are written around AI SDK message parts; if you stream from another SDK you will write the mapping yourself. The release is days old, so expect APIs and examples to move, and remember that copied code does not update on its own. And showing raw reasoning is a product decision as well as a design one: the shadcn Reasoning demo collapses the text into “Thought for 5s” once the step finishes, which is a sensible default.

## How to adopt it this week

- **List every step type your agent emits.** Reasoning, tool calls, sources, plans, subagents, errors, approvals. If one does not fit “icon + title + status + optional detail”, question it before designing a new widget.

- **Write titles as past-tense sentences.** Present tense while running, past tense when done, and say the failure in words. That one rule fixes most screen-reader and scanning problems.

- **Open while running, collapse when done.** The demos open a line while the step streams and fold it afterwards; the person can still expand it.

- **Put output in a small Code Block, never in the sentence.** Commands, logs and diffs go inside the line’s expanded content at `size="sm"`.

- **Keep approvals out of the trace.** Ask with an explicit Deny / Approve item; record the decision as a normal line afterwards.

- **Test the states, not just the happy path.** Running, error, pending, nested, a very long title, keyboard-only, reduced motion, light and dark.

```
# install
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add trace
pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add code-block

# let your coding agent read the pattern
Add the Reasoning pattern from https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/ai-elements/base/reasoning.md to my chat.

# map message parts to lines
reasoning  → "Thinking" / "Thought for 5s", collapsible
tool call  → "Running <cmd>" / "Ran <cmd>" / "Failed to run <cmd>", output in Code Block sm
source     → link line, "(opens in a new tab)" in sr-only text
approval   → Confirmation item outside Trace, then a Tool line
```

## Where UI Hub fits

Trace and Code Block cover the activity inside a turn; the rest of the page still needs a direction. Browse the 
chat
 component kind in the UI Hub resource list for other agent and chat libraries to compare against, and pair them with the restrained look in our 
shadcn Blocks deep dive
. If your agent also restyles your system, the same week shadcndesign turned its DS Manager into an MCP server, so a coding agent can change a shadcn theme while respecting locked values.

# Lovart 2.0 and Arti: design agents learn to remember, run and review

> Lovart 2.0 adds an editable taste memory, scheduled design delegation and a background consistency check. Read alongside two other launches from 19 Oct, it shows where design agents are heading, and what you should write down before you hand one the work.

Blog post: <https://siinxu.github.io/ui-resource-hub/blog/lovart-arti-design-agent-memory/>

On 19 October Lovart shipped version 2.0 of its design agent, built around a new personal agent called Arti. The pitch is not a better image model. Lovart already routes to several third-party image and video models. The change is everything around generation: Arti keeps a memory of how you work, takes whole jobs on a schedule, researches before you start and checks the canvas while you work. It is a useful snapshot of where design agents are going, and of what you have to write down before you can trust one with real work.

## What actually shipped

- **Memory you can read and edit.** Lovart splits memory into four groups: basic information, collaboration style, aesthetic preferences and frequently used assets. Each entry can be viewed, edited or deleted, you choose whether it applies across projects, and you can seed it by chatting, from past projects, or by uploading a portfolio or a Markdown or memory file from another AI tool.

- **Design delegation.** Instead of a chain of prompts you write a brief (what to make, what to watch for, what done looks like), pick the target project, then run it once or daily, weekly or monthly. Each run has a credit limit, there is a Test run before you commit, and results land on a new canvas page. Lovart's own example: 168 product images for 42 SKUs in four sizes, run overnight after a four-SKU test.

- **Design Research and Design Review.** Research gathers references from sources such as Google, Pinterest and Behance into a report with a mood board. Review checks the canvas against the project's constraints in the background and only changes anything after you confirm. Lovart's example is a hand-drawn storyboard with one oil-paint frame that slipped through.

- **Self-evolving skills.** When you repeat the same workflow across projects more than three times, Lovart offers to save it as a reusable skill. You can switch this off.

## The same week, the same idea elsewhere

Two smaller launches on the same day point the same way. Gemini Notebook added a Review toggle so you can read and edit the outline or producer notes for slides and video overviews 
before
 anything renders. Automo's design engine now has a creative-director judge that looks at several rendered candidates and keeps the strongest, and its thumbs-up and thumbs-down now attach to the exact design you rated. Put together, the pattern is clear. The value is moving from "generate" to three other steps: remember what the person likes, show the plan before spending compute, and judge the output against something other than the average of the training data.

## Our take

Memory is only as good as what is in it. A vague "I like clean, modern design" in memory produces the same generic result as a vague prompt, now on every project. The strongest line in Lovart's announcement is its own example memory: show three clearly different directions first, then build out the one I pick. That is a process rule, and process rules are what agents follow well. Treat the memory panel the way we treat a guideline file: short, specific and testable. The Review step is promising for the same reason. A consistency check needs explicit constraints to check against, so write them down at the start of the project rather than hoping the agent infers them.

Delegation is where the real risk is. A weekly job that quietly drifts off-brand is worse than no job. Lovart's guardrails (test run, credit limit, results on a separate canvas page, run history, pause) are the right shape, and you should use all of them.

## Checklist: before you hand a design agent the work

- **Write the taste memory by hand.** Three to six lines: palette in named values, type pairing, density, two or three references, and a never-list. Upload it as Markdown instead of letting the agent guess from old projects.

- **Add one process rule.** For example "three distinct directions first, then build out the chosen one", or "always show the outline before rendering".

- **State constraints the reviewer can check.** Style, aspect ratios, logo clear space, text-on-image contrast. If it is not written, no background check can catch it.

- **Test before you schedule.** Run a small batch (Lovart's own example used 4 of 42 SKUs), read every output, then set the schedule and a credit cap.

- **Read the memory panel monthly.** Delete anything stale or wrong. Learned preferences are guesses until you confirm them.

- **Keep the final call.** Accept fixes one by one, the way Lovart's Review asks you to, and never let a scheduled run publish straight to a live channel.

```
# taste.md (upload as memory)
palette: cream #f6f1e7 · ink #1d1a16 · one accent, warm brown #8a5a3b
type: serif headlines + neutral sans body; no more than two weights
density: generous white space; one focal image per layout
process: show 3 clearly different directions first, then build the chosen one
never: neon gradients · stock 3D blobs · emoji as icons · text over busy photos
check: same illustration style on every frame · logo clear space ≥ 1× cap height
```

## How UI Hub helps

If you are writing that taste file from scratch, start from the house-style notes and specs in the 
UI Hub encyclopedia
, and our earlier piece on 
teaching agents taste
. The format is the same whether the agent is Lovart, Claude, Cursor or Figma's: short rules first, pixels second.

## References

- [Lovart](https://www.lovart.ai/) — Lovart
